content: Chronic cystic mastitis, also referred to as fibrocystic breast changes, is a condition characterized by painful and lumpy breasts. Below is a detailed explanation of the symptoms, causes, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis associated with this condition: Symptoms of Chronic Cystic Mastitis: 1. Symptoms often improve after menopause. Women taking birth control pills may experience fewer symptoms, while those on hormone therapy may notice an increase in symptoms. 2. Symptoms are typically worse just before menstruation and tend to improve once the period begins. 3. Common symptoms include: Pain or discomfort in both breasts, which may fluctuate with the menstrual cycle but can persist throughout the month. Breasts that feel full, swollen, and heavy. Pain or discomfort extending to the underarm area. Thickened or lumpy breast tissue. A lump in the breast that enlarges before each period and reduces in size afterward. This type of lump is mobile when pressed and does not feel fixed to the surrounding tissue. Such lumps are commonly associated with fibrocystic breast changes. Nipple discharge may occur. If the discharge is clear, red, or bloody, it is important to consult a healthcare provider immediately. Causes of Chronic Cystic Mastitis: 1. The exact cause of this condition is unknown. However, it is believed that ovarian hormones play a role in causing the breasts to feel swollen, lumpy, or painful before or during menstruation. 2. Up to 50% of women experience this condition at some point in their lives, with the highest prevalence occurring between the ages of 20 and 45. It is rare in postmenopausal women unless they are taking estrogen. 3. Some women report that consuming chocolate, caffeine, or high-fat foods exacerbates their symptoms, but there is no definitive evidence to support this. Diagnosis: 1. A healthcare provider will perform a physical examination, including a breast exam. It is important to inform the provider of any noticeable breast changes. 2. Women over the age of 40 should discuss with their doctor how often they should undergo mammograms to screen for breast cancer. 3. For women under 35, a breast ultrasound may be used to examine the breast tissue more closely. 4. If a lump is detected during a breast exam or if a mammogram result is abnormal, additional tests may be required. These may include another mammogram or a breast ultrasound. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: 1. Contact your healthcare provider if you notice new or unusual lumps during a breast self-exam. 2. Seek immediate medical attention if you experience new nipple discharge, especially if it is bloody or clear. 3. Report any redness, puckering of the skin, or flattening/indentation of the nipple to your healthcare provider. Treatment Options: 1. Women with no symptoms or only mild symptoms typically do not require treatment. 2. Self-care measures recommended by healthcare providers may include: Taking over-the-counter pain relievers such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen. Applying heat or ice to the breasts. Wearing a well-fitting or sports bra for support. Some women believe that reducing fat, caffeine, or chocolate intake helps alleviate symptoms, but there is no strong evidence to confirm this. Supplements such as vitamin E, thiamine, magnesium, and evening primrose oil are generally safe but have not been proven effective. 3. For more severe symptoms, a healthcare provider may prescribe hormones, such as birth control pills or other medications. It is important to take these medications exactly as directed and report any side effects to the provider. 4. Surgery is not a treatment option for this condition. Prognosis: 1. If breast exams and mammograms are normal, there is no need to worry about the symptoms. 2. Fibrocystic breast changes do not increase the risk of breast cancer. 3. Symptoms usually improve after menopause. This information provides a comprehensive understanding of chronic cystic mastitis and its management. Always consult a healthcare provider for personalized advice and treatment.
